payload.snippet: You are shopping with your elderly grandparent who experiences a dizzy spell near the chilled aisle and sits down on the floor.
options: Alert a store first-aider and wait with your grandparent calmly
Continue shopping and come back to check later
Help them up quickly and carry on shopping
Run outside for help and leave them alone
payload.explanation: Stores have trained first-aiders — alerting them immediately is the safest first step.

payload.snippet: The online grocery delivery arrived with two substituted items significantly more expensive than the originals and the driver is asking for a payment top-up at the door.
options: Reject the expensive substitutions and request a refund through the app
Pay the top-up to avoid any conflict and forget it
Call the shop while the driver waits to dispute the charge
Accept the substitutions and file a claim the following week
payload.explanation: Substitution upcharges at the door are not legally required — you may reject them under standard online grocery terms.

payload.snippet: The family budget is nearly exhausted and the weekly shopping list has twelve non-essential items added by habit without checking the balance.
options: Remove the non-essentials and stick to a revised list before checkout
Buy everything and worry about it next month
Use a credit card to cover the overspend this week
Ask the cashier to stop scanning at a random point in the list
payload.explanation: Removing non-essentials before checkout is the responsible move that avoids building up credit dependency.

payload.snippet: The shop charged correctly for each item but the automatic meal-deal discount was not applied to any of the five lunches you selected under the deal rules.
options: Show the receipt at customer services and request all five discounts back at once
Accept the loss on all five items quietly
Queue again at the original till to dispute each item one by one
Film the shelf label and post it on social media immediately
payload.explanation: Customer services can apply all five missed deal discounts at once with the receipt and a quick shelf-label check.

payload.snippet: The supermarket car park barrier has trapped your car after the free parking time ran out while you queued at the pharmacy counter.
options: Explain to the pay-point manager and show the pharmacy receipt
Pay the full penalty charge without any question
Argue with the barrier and refuse to pay at all
Call the car park company from inside the trapped car
payload.explanation: Pharmacy receipts showing the wait time are accepted as evidence of unavoidable delay at most supermarket car parks.

payload.snippet: Your teenager has scanned a significant item at self-checkout but walked out while it was still sitting on the bag scale and has not been charged.
options: Return to the till immediately and pay for the item
Leave because the machine should have charged it automatically
Pay only half to settle a fair share of the error
Tell the shop on the next visit instead
payload.explanation: Returning to pay is the only honest and legal response to an accidental checkout error however it happened.

payload.snippet: The shop's price matcher has declined to match a lower competitor price saying the product is a slightly different weight variant that excludes it from the terms.
options: Check the per-unit price of both before deciding whether to buy
Leave the shop in frustration without anything
Buy the item at full price without any further check
Demand a manager override the terms and conditions
payload.explanation: Per-unit price comparison is the correct test when a size difference is cited to refuse a price match.

payload.snippet: A staff member is restocking the top shelf with heavy boxes using a ladder directly above the aisle where you need the cereal.
options: Wait safely nearby until the restock is finished
Walk quickly under the ladder before anything can fall
Ask the staff member to stop and let you through
Reach around the base of the ladder while they work above
payload.explanation: Waiting clear of an active overhead restock is the safest and correct behaviour in any shop.

payload.snippet: The shop security alarm has triggered as you walk out with a properly purchased jacket and the receipt is inside your bag.
options: Stop calmly and show the receipt and item to the security guard
Run because you know you have paid correctly
Shout at the security guard about the alarm going off
Drop the bag and walk quickly to the car instead
payload.explanation: Stopping calmly and providing the receipt is both the legal requirement and the fastest way to resolve a security alarm trigger.

payload.snippet: Your shopping trolley and handbag were left near the frozen section while you went back for a missed item and the handbag has been moved on your return.
options: Report it to security immediately and check the contents
Assume the bag just fell and continue shopping
Continue shopping and check everything at home later
Ask nearby shoppers if they saw anything and then continue
payload.explanation: Immediate security reporting triggers CCTV review while the footage is still current — waiting reduces the chance of recovery.

payload.snippet: A fellow shopper has accused you loudly of queue-jumping at the deli counter and you are certain you arrived before them based on the ticket system.
options: Show the ticket number and let the deli staff adjudicate calmly
Argue back loudly in front of everyone nearby
Give up your turn to end the conflict quickly
Call the shop manager to the counter immediately
payload.explanation: The ticket system is the objective record — showing the ticket and letting staff rule is the correct and calm response.

payload.snippet: The family weekly shop has been inflated by introductory prices reverting to full price with no shelf notice to warn shoppers.
options: Compare the receipt to last week's and query the reversions with the manager
Accept all the price rises silently without checking
Switch every item to a cheaper brand immediately without checking
Leave the shop and file an online complaint that evening
payload.explanation: Comparing receipts plus a manager query often results in a transitional discount and flags the missing shelf notices.

payload.snippet: You have discovered a large shopping bag left under the till by the previous customer as you load your items onto the belt.
options: Hand it to the cashier immediately
Look inside and keep any useful items for yourself
Leave the bag for the next person in the queue
Carry it out to the car park to find the owner yourself
payload.explanation: Handing to the cashier triggers the lost-property system and gets the bag back to its owner most efficiently.

payload.snippet: The cashier has begun packing your items without asking if you have a loyalty card and the transaction is already partway through.
options: Ask the cashier to pause and enter your card number now
Accept the missed points and move on without asking
Ask for the whole transaction to be cancelled and restarted
Show your card number on the phone screen without asking
payload.explanation: Most loyalty systems allow mid-transaction card entry — a quick ask to the cashier resolves it without a restart.

payload.snippet: Your reusable bags were left at home and the shop has run out of carrier bags mid-shift leaving only thin produce bags available.
options: Use the trolley to load items directly into the car boot and pack from there
Balance everything loose in your arms across the car park
Leave the shopping at the door and call a taxi home
Stack items directly in the back seat with no bags at all
payload.explanation: Loading directly from the trolley into the car then packing properly saves every item without needing a single bag.

payload.snippet: The self-checkout has asked for ID for the wine but the ID-checker is occupied with another customer and you are in a rush.
options: Wait for the ID check however long it takes
Place the wine back and leave without it today
Hand your ID to the cashier in the next aisle over
Use the self-checkout at a less busy time instead
payload.explanation: Age verification is a legal requirement — waiting is the only lawful option however inconvenient the timing.

payload.snippet: The budget tin of tomatoes you always buy has doubled in price and is now more expensive than the premium brand on the shelf right beside it.
options: Check the premium brand size and unit cost before buying
Buy the budget tin anyway out of long-standing habit
Skip tinned tomatoes entirely this week as a protest
Ask the cashier why the price changed as you pay
payload.explanation: Unit-price comparison is the correct move when a budget label becomes more expensive than its premium neighbour.

payload.snippet: The receipt shows your loyalty card points promotion was applied at the wrong tier and the saving on the full weekly shop is more than twenty pounds less than it should be.
options: Return to customer services with the receipt and the promotion terms
Accept the difference as a misunderstanding and go home
Come back next week when it is less busy to query it
Post the receipt photograph online and wait for the retailer to respond
payload.explanation: Customer services with clear evidence can apply the correct tier saving on the same visit using the promotion terms.

payload.snippet: The in-store pharmacy has dispensed the wrong prescription item and you only notice the error when you open the package at home one hour after leaving.
options: Call the pharmacy immediately and return the wrong item unopened
Take the wrong medication anyway until the correct one arrives
Throw it away and order a fresh prescription from scratch
Ask a neighbour who takes the same drug whether they want it
payload.explanation: Calling immediately and returning the unopened package triggers the dispensing error protocol and ensures you get the correct item safely.

payload.snippet: Your eight-year-old has been consistently taking more than ninety minutes to fall asleep every single night for the past six months despite a calm and consistent routine.
options: Consult a sleep specialist and trial a gradual bedtime restriction protocol
Move bedtime to midnight to match the child's natural sleep time
Remove the bedtime routine entirely and let the child self-settle
Give the child melatonin from the chemist without a doctor's advice
payload.explanation: Six months of long sleep-onset delay requires specialist review — bedtime restriction is the evidence-based first treatment.

payload.snippet: A teenager's sleep has shifted so dramatically that they cannot wake before noon and cannot sleep before 2am despite months of trying to shift earlier.
options: See a GP for a circadian rhythm assessment and trial light therapy in the morning
Accept the schedule and move the teenager to an evening-only school timetable
Force a 7am wake-up every day regardless of sleep time
Tell the teenager they are being lazy and refuse to engage
payload.explanation: Delayed sleep phase syndrome is a recognised condition that responds to morning light therapy and GP-guided intervention.

payload.snippet: The family has bought a new mattress but after two weeks everyone's sleep quality has dropped and back pain has appeared.
options: Return or exchange the mattress using the trial period and get independent advice on firmness
Keep the mattress and add a thick soft topper
Dispose of the mattress and sleep on the floor
Continue for three months to see if the body adjusts
payload.explanation: New mattresses have return periods — using the trial period is far cheaper than absorbing back pain and fatigue.

payload.snippet: Your child has been prescribed melatonin by a GP but you are worried about giving a supplement long-term to a seven-year-old.
options: Discuss your concerns with the GP and ask about a time-limited trial with reassessment
Stop the melatonin the day after starting without telling the GP
Double the dose to get the child asleep faster and taper sooner
Search for melatonin gummies online and swap to those instead
payload.explanation: GP-prescribed melatonin for children is monitored and short-term — discussing concerns openly is the right approach.

payload.snippet: Your partner and you have incompatible sleep schedules and it is causing significant tension in the relationship and household.
options: Discuss a compromise that preserves each person's core sleep need and trial separate duvets
Demand your partner match your schedule or sleep separately permanently
Take turns sleeping in the living room by week
Accept permanent tension as the price of different schedules
payload.explanation: Separate duvets plus a compromise overlap window is the most effective solution for mismatched sleep schedules.

payload.snippet: A child in the family has night terrors several times a week and is impossible to wake or comfort during the episode.
options: Do not wake during the terror — clear the space and note the usual time
Shake the child awake mid-terror to stop the episode
Video the episode and post it online for advice
Insist the child stays awake until the terror time passes every night
payload.explanation: Night terrors resolve on their own — forcing waking increases distress without benefit.

payload.snippet: You are sharing a hotel room with a colleague at a conference and your colleague snores loudly enough to wake you multiple times.
options: Use earplugs and politely mention it in the morning
Snore back to drown them out
Ask the conference team to reassign you at 3am
Poke your colleague awake every time they snore
payload.explanation: Earplugs plus a quiet morning mention is the polite and practical solution to shared-room snoring.

payload.snippet: A child has been bedwetting after two dry years and the family is unsure whether to punish or ignore it.
options: See the GP — do not punish bedwetting after dry years as it often has a medical cause
Restrict all fluids from 4pm onwards without GP guidance
Put the child back in nappies without discussing it with them
Punish to create a stronger incentive to stay dry
payload.explanation: Regression after two dry years is a medical indicator, not a behaviour problem — punishment is actively harmful.

payload.snippet: You have started a new shift pattern that means you sleep from 7am to 3pm and the whole house is disrupted by noise and light during your sleep hours.
options: Fit blackout curtains, add a white noise machine, and discuss quiet hours with the family
Insist the entire family changes their routine permanently
Sleep in the garden shed to get complete quiet
Quit the shift pattern because sleep quality matters more
payload.explanation: Blackout plus white noise plus a family quiet-hour agreement protects the shift worker without displacing the household.

payload.snippet: Your child is consistently overtired at school and the teacher has asked for a meeting about drowsiness in class.
options: Track bedtime and wake time for a week and share the log at the meeting
Tell the teacher to let the child sleep at the desk
Blame the school's early start time and take no action
Move to home schooling to allow a later wake-up
payload.explanation: A one-week sleep log gives the teacher and family a factual basis for a constructive conversation.

payload.snippet: The family has just adopted a rescue dog that howls for several hours every night for the first week.
options: Set up a comfort crate near your bed with a worn item of clothing inside
Rehome the dog after three nights
Let the dog cry it out regardless of duration each night
Keep the dog in the garden so the howling is less audible
payload.explanation: A familiar-scent item in a crate near humans significantly shortens the settling period for a newly adopted dog.

payload.snippet: You have been taking sleep medication prescribed three years ago and you now cannot sleep at all without it even on holiday.
options: Speak to your GP about a gradual supervised withdrawal plan
Stop the medication abruptly this week
Double the dose when sleep is particularly poor
Order a different sleep aid online without a prescription
payload.explanation: Long-term sleep medication creates dependency — a GP-guided gradual taper is far safer than abrupt stopping.

payload.snippet: Your child wakes at exactly 5:30am every morning and joins you in bed until 7am and neither of you gets quality sleep in that window.
options: Install a colour-change clock that shows when it is okay to get up
Start waking at 5:30 so the child has company
Lock the bedroom door and tell the child to wait silently
Move the alarm to 5:30 and start the whole day early
payload.explanation: Colour-change clocks give children a concrete visual cue and dramatically reduce early wake intrusions.

payload.snippet: A parent has begun working night shifts and the family is struggling to keep quiet during the day while they sleep.
options: Create a clear quiet-zone map of the house during sleep hours and use headphones
Ask the employer to move back to day shifts immediately
Have the entire family leave the house all day
Build a soundproofed room for the sleeping parent
payload.explanation: A visual quiet zone map plus headphones preserves normal family activity while protecting the sleep space.

payload.snippet: A ten-year-old has developed a strong fear of the dark after watching a frightening film at a friend's house.
options: Introduce a gradual darkness reduction plan and validate the fear without amplifying it
Force total darkness immediately to overcome the fear faster
Leave the full overhead light on indefinitely
Punish the child for being scared of the dark at their age
payload.explanation: Gradual desensitisation with validation is the evidence-based approach to acquired fear of the dark.

payload.snippet: The couple's newborn wakes every two to three hours and both parents are becoming dangerously sleep deprived after six weeks.
options: Arrange at least one four-to-five hour unbroken sleep block per parent per night
Push through and accept exhaustion as the price of parenthood
Let the newborn self-settle from six weeks old
Give the newborn formula to stretch the sleep window without advice
payload.explanation: A minimum four-hour unbroken block per adult per night is the medical threshold for preventing severe sleep deprivation effects.

payload.snippet: Your teenager has been coming home from parties at 2am and sleeping until 2pm and the household routine is collapsing.
options: Agree a realistic home time and enforce a morning alarm even on weekends
Lock the teenager out if they arrive after midnight
Let the weekend pattern continue and restart routine at school term start
Move the family's entire schedule to match the teenager's hours
payload.explanation: A consistent morning alarm even on weekend nights limits the degree of sleep schedule drift.

payload.snippet: You have been relying on caffeine to stay alert because your sleep has been consistently under five hours a night for three months.
options: See your GP about the root cause of short sleep rather than masking it with caffeine
Increase caffeine to get through the day while continuing to sleep five hours
Switch to energy drinks for a stronger effect
Take naps whenever possible and ignore the night sleep issue
payload.explanation: Three months of under-five-hour sleep is a medical concern — caffeine masking delays addressing the root cause.

payload.snippet: A young child has developed an elaborate delaying bedtime routine involving multiple stuffed toys each needing individual goodnight rituals.
options: Agree a fixed number of goodnights and hold the limit consistently
Allow every ritual because the child needs the security
Abruptly cancel all toys and goodnight rituals overnight
Start the routine two hours earlier to absorb the delay
payload.explanation: A fixed agreed number of goodnights gives predictability while preventing the ritual from expanding indefinitely.

payload.snippet: Your family is preparing for the clocks-change weekend and the children always suffer a week of disturbed sleep afterwards.
options: Shift bedtime by fifteen minutes earlier each day for four days before the change
Change bedtime by the full hour on the night itself
Ignore the clock change and deal with it as it happens
Keep children on the old time all year regardless of the clocks
payload.explanation: Four fifteen-minute shifts spread the one-hour adjustment across the days before the change arrives.

payload.snippet: A teenager on your street has been posting increasingly concerning messages on social media suggesting they feel hopeless and that nobody cares about them.
options: Contact a trusted adult immediately and share the messages — do not wait to see if they get better
Send a heart emoji to show you care
Tell the teenager to cheer up in a reply
Wait until the next day to see if the mood passes
payload.explanation: Signs of hopelessness in a teenager's public posts are a mental health alert that adults trained in safeguarding must be told about immediately.

payload.snippet: Your colleague has disclosed to you privately that they are in a financially abusive relationship and their partner controls all the money but they have not asked for help.
options: Listen without judgement, share the domestic abuse helpline number, and let them lead
T
payload.explanation: Listening and sharing a helpline number preserves the person's agency and safety — acting without their consent in an abusive situation can escalate danger.

payload.snippet: A long-term volunteer in your charity has been making increasingly negative and discouraging comments to newer volunteers and morale is dropping noticeably.
options: Have a private, honest and respectful conversation with the volunteer about the impact of their comments
Ask the volunteer to leave immediately
Complain about the volunteer to the whole team
Ignore it because they have been there the longest
payload.explanation: A direct private conversation addresses the behaviour early enough to preserve both the volunteer and the team.

payload.snippet: You have discovered that an elderly neighbour has been the victim of a doorstep scam and has handed over three thousand pounds to a person claiming to be from a utility company.
options: Help them report it to Action Fraud and their bank today and contact social services for a vulnerability check
Tell the neighbour they should have known better
Post about it on the street social media group
Call the utility company yourself to sort it out
payload.explanation: Action Fraud plus a bank report plus a social services vulnerability check are all standard simultaneous responses to elder financial abuse.

payload.snippet: A friend has asked you to write a glowing reference for a job they want but you genuinely have concerns about their suitability for that specific role.
options: Have an honest conversation with your friend before writing any reference
Write a dishonest glowing reference to help them get the job
Decline without explanation to avoid the conversation
Write a critical reference without telling them
payload.explanation: A dishonest reference can cause serious harm if the person is placed in a role they are not suitable for — honesty before writing protects both friend and employer.

payload.snippet: Your charity's biggest donor has asked for special treatment that conflicts with the charity's equal-access policy in exchange for their next donation.
options: Decline the special treatment politely and explain the equal-access policy to the donor
Accept the condition because the donation is too large to lose
Make an informal exception and do not record it
Resign rather than deal with the pressure
payload.explanation: Charity policies must be upheld even with major donors — accepting conditional gifts with access conditions breaches equal-service obligations.

payload.snippet: A community food bank you run has discovered that one regular client has been taking supplies significantly beyond the agreed limit over several months.
options: Have a dignified private conversation to understand the situation before taking any action
Announce the rule breach to all volunteers
Remove the client from the food bank immediately
Increase the limit for everyone to be fair
payload.explanation: A private conversation first often reveals genuine need that the existing rules did not account for — dignity is the first principle of food bank operation.

payload.snippet: Your organisation is running a community helpline and a caller has disclosed that they are currently caring for a child while intoxicated.
options: Follow the safeguarding protocol and make a referral to children's services while the caller is still on the line
Tell the caller to sober up and call back
Advise the caller to call a friend to cover
Log the call and escalate to the supervisor after the shift
payload.explanation: An in-call safeguarding referral is the only response that acts in the child's interest while the situation is live.

payload.snippet: You are a teacher and a student has disclosed that their parent is seriously ill at home and there is nobody else to care for a younger sibling.
options: Inform the pastoral lead immediately and contact the local authority family support service
Tell the student to call extended family and solve it themselves
Keep it confidential and monitor how the student manages
Ask the student to bring the younger sibling to school
payload.explanation: Teachers are mandatory reporters — a pastoral lead plus a family support referral are the correct dual responses to a child in a vulnerable home situation.

payload.snippet: A community centre in your area is facing closure because it lacks a treasurer and no one has applied despite several public appeals over the past six months.
options: Volunteer for a fixed term of twelve months even if you do not plan to continue beyond that
Wait for someone with better skills to apply
Decline because you might not be available in a year
Suggest the centre applies for a grant to pay a professional
payload.explanation: A fixed-term volunteer commitment prevents the closure while creating time to recruit a permanent solution.

payload.snippet: A friend has been crowd-funding for a personal cause and has privately told you they will not reach their target and have promised the recipient they would cover a specific cost regardless.
options: Offer to make a private contribution that closes the gap rather than promote the campaign further
Continue sharing the campaign and hope it reaches target
Tell the friend they should not have made a promise they could not keep
Ask the recipient to reduce their expectation
payload.explanation: A private contribution that closes the gap is the most direct and dignified help when a friend has made a commitment they cannot meet alone.

payload.snippet: You have been asked to mentor a young person from a disadvantaged background and you are well-qualified for the role but your own schedule is genuinely very full.
options: Commit to one meeting a month with clear boundaries rather than agreeing to more than you can sustain
Decline because you cannot give the full commitment
Agree to weekly meetings even though the schedule will not hold
Say yes to everything and manage it as it comes
payload.explanation: A sustainable commitment with honest boundaries is more valuable to a mentee than an enthusiastic start that collapses.

payload.snippet: Your office kitchen has been left in a consistently poor state by unknown colleagues and it is affecting everyone's comfort at work.
options: Put up a respectful note and be the one who sets the example by cleaning up after yourself
Report it to management as a formal complaint
Tell every colleague you suspect directly
Stop using the kitchen yourself as a protest
payload.explanation: Leading by example plus a respectful note sets the tone without creating conflict over an unproven individual.

payload.snippet: A volunteer visitor to a residential care home has told you that one of the staff members is routinely dismissive and cold toward the residents they do not like.
options: Report the specific observed incidents to the care home manager and the local CQC inspector
Tell the staff member directly what you have observed
Post about it on social media to raise awareness
Stay quiet because it is not officially your responsibility
payload.explanation: Cold and dismissive treatment of care home residents is a dignity and safeguarding concern — reporting to the manager and CQC creates an audit trail.

payload.snippet: A colleague you supervise has told you that they have been struggling with alcohol dependency and has asked for your confidence and for no changes to be made to their responsibilities.
options: Acknowledge the trust, support them in accessing occupational health, and agree a brief monitoring plan
Tell them their job is safe as long as they keep it secret
Report to HR immediately without the employee's knowledge
Promise to say nothing and take no further action
payload.explanation: Supporting access to occupational health protects both the employee and the people they serve — doing nothing is not a safe option.

payload.snippet: Your neighbour's adult child has asked you to keep an eye on the elderly parent while they are away for a month and you realise partway through that the parent has a fall and cannot get up.
options: Call 999 and stay with the parent until help arrives, then contact the adult child
Help the parent up yourself before calling anyone
Wait to see if the parent gets up on their own
Call the adult child first and wait for instructions
payload.explanation: Calling 999 immediately is the correct response to a person who cannot get up after a fall — a GP or paramedic must assess for injury before any movement.

payload.snippet: A teenager at your youth club has told you they are experiencing racist abuse from a group in the area and does not want to involve the police because of a previous negative experience.
options: Listen carefully, record the incidents in detail, and explore with them whether reporting through the school or a specialist organisation feels safer
Report to the police yourself without the teenager's consent
Tell the teenager the police are the only option
Minimise the incidents to avoid making the teenager more fearful
payload.explanation: Supporting the teenager to choose a reporting route they trust is more likely to lead to protective action than overriding their concerns.

payload.snippet: You have been asked to give a character reference in a custody dispute between two people you know well and both parties have requested your support separately without knowing you know the other.
options: Decline to give a reference in a contested case where you know both parties
Write a reference supporting the person who asked first
Write separate references for both parties without telling either
Write one balanced reference covering both
payload.explanation: Giving a reference in a contested custody case where you know both parties creates a conflict of interest that cannot be managed — declining is the only ethical position.

payload.snippet: A classmate has confided that they have been sending money to someone they met online who they believe is a romantic partner but who you suspect is running a romance fraud.
options: Share your concern gently and suggest showing the conversation to a trusted adult or Action Fraud
Tell the classmate they are being stupid and naive
Report it to Action Fraud yourself without telling the classmate
Introduce your classmate to someone else to distract them
payload.explanation: A gentle concern shared alongside a trusted resource is more likely to be heard than a blunt accusation when someone is emotionally invested in the situation.

payload.snippet: A parent at your child's school has disclosed that their family is living in a car after losing their housing and they have begged you not to tell anyone because they are afraid their children will be taken into care.
options: Gently explain that the council has a duty to help and that housing support is separate from child protection, then help them contact the council housing emergency line
Promise to tell nobody and give them some cash
Tell the school immediately without the parent's knowledge
Offer your own spare room without taking any further steps
payload.explanation: Correcting the misconception about child protection and actively supporting a referral to housing is both truthful and immediately practical.

payload.snippet: A business partnership of several years is dissolving and both partners believe they contributed more than half the value and neither will accept less than fifty-five percent of the assets.
options: Appoint a neutral mediator and agree in advance to accept the mediator's recommended split
Litigate immediately to protect your position
Accept fifty percent now and sue later for the difference
Stall all discussions until one partner gives up
payload.explanation: A pre-agreed neutral mediator is faster and cheaper than litigation and avoids the relationship damage of a prolonged dispute.

payload.snippet: Two departments in a company are both claiming the same budget line and each manager has separately promised their team the funding is secured.
options: Escalate jointly to the CFO with both business cases rather than competing through informal lobbying
Campaign internally for your own department's version only
Wait for the other manager to back down under pressure
Spend the budget immediately before the dispute is resolved
payload.explanation: A joint escalation with both cases presents the CFO with all the information needed to make a fair and informed decision quickly.

payload.snippet: Your teenage child has been offered a place at a prestigious school that would require the family to move city but your partner's career is based in the current city.
options: Hold a family meeting that includes the child, acknowledge all interests equally, and explore all options before deciding
Make the decision based purely on the child's school place
Make the decision based purely on the partner's career
Let the child decide alone because it is their education
payload.explanation: A family decision of this scale requires every person's interests to be genuinely considered before any option is closed.

payload.snippet: A close friend has borrowed a meaningful sum of money with a clear repayment date that has now passed by three months and they have not mentioned it.
options: Raise it directly and kindly — ask if there is a problem you can help with and set a new date together
Write off the loan to save the friendship
Issue a formal demand without any conversation first
Tell mutual friends about the unpaid loan
payload.explanation: A direct conversation acknowledges both the financial reality and the friendship, which a silent write-off or legal threat would both damage.

payload.snippet: Three siblings have inherited a family home that one sibling lives in and the other two want to sell, but the resident sibling cannot afford to buy the others out at current market value.
options: Seek independent legal advice on a deferred sale or equity release arrangement that gives the resident sibling time
Force an immediate sale at market value
Give the resident sibling the house and waive your share
Leave the dispute unresolved for years while costs accumulate
payload.explanation: Legal mechanisms such as a deferred sale or equity release can protect the resident sibling while giving the other two a clear timeline for their inheritance.

payload.snippet: A community fundraising group has split into two factions with irreconcilable views on what the raised money should fund and neither faction will compromise.
options: Propose a transparent vote of all members with a clear majority threshold and commit to accepting the result
Give all the money to the faction whose cause you prefer
Split the money equally between both causes without a vote
Dissolve the group and return all donations to donors
payload.explanation: A transparent member vote with a pre-agreed threshold is the only democratic mechanism that gives both factions a fair chance.

payload.snippet: Your employer has asked you to share confidential client information with a new team member who will work on the account, but the client had previously expressed reservations about their data being seen by additional staff.
options: Tell your employer about the client's stated concern before sharing and request guidance
Share the information without telling the employer about the client's concern
Refuse to share entirely without discussing it with your employer
Share only a redacted version without telling either party
payload.explanation: Flagging the client's concern to the employer before sharing protects you, the employer, and the client relationship from an avoidable breach of trust.

payload.snippet: A divorced couple shares custody of a child and one parent consistently makes last-minute schedule changes that disrupt the other parent's plans and work commitments.
options: Request a mediated conversation to add a minimum-notice clause to the custody arrangement
Stop accommodating any change however urgent
Return every last-minute change with one of your own
Use the changes as grounds to apply for sole custody
payload.explanation: A minimum-notice clause formalised through mediation gives both parents a concrete tool to manage disruptions without returning to court.

payload.snippet: A household of five students shares utility bills equally but one student works from home all day using far more energy than the others who are out at university.
options: Agree a weighted contribution based on actual at-home hours as estimated by a group discussion
Force the work-from-home student to pay the entire bill alone
Continue equal splits and absorb the higher cost silently
Install a sub-meter for the work-from-home student's room
payload.explanation: A group-agreed weighted contribution is fairer than equal splits when usage is clearly unequal, and more proportionate than full liability.

payload.snippet: A family trust has been managing a family property for decades and two beneficiaries have diametrically opposing views on whether to sell in the current market or hold for ten more years.
options: Commission an independent property valuation and financial projection and commit to deciding by the trust's next formal meeting
Make the decision without telling the dissenting beneficiary
Ignore the matter until the disagreement resolves itself
Remove the dissenting beneficiary from the trust decision
payload.explanation: An independent valuation gives both sides a shared factual basis for the decision and removes the argument from pure personal preference.

payload.snippet: A community sports club has one pitch and two teams both have equal historical claim to the prime Saturday afternoon slot but only one can use it each week.
options: Establish a seasonal alternating system where each team gets the prime slot for half the season
Give the slot permanently to the higher-ranked team
Hold a coin flip every week which satisfies neither team long-term
Split the pitch down the middle so both teams practice simultaneously
payload.explanation: A seasonal alternating system gives both teams a reliable prime slot for half the year — predictable and equally weighted.

payload.snippet: Your employer has made you aware that a colleague in another team earns thirty percent more for work that is essentially equivalent to yours.
options: Raise the pay disparity directly in a formal pay review with evidence of the comparable work
Leak the colleague's salary to others to create pressure
Reduce your effort to match what you are paid relative to the colleague
Accept the disparity and say nothing because your contract is confidential
payload.explanation: A formal pay review with evidence of comparable work is the correct internal mechanism for addressing a pay disparity before considering any external options.

payload.snippet: Two adult children are disagreeing about how much home care their increasingly frail parent needs and one adult child who lives nearby is bearing most of the burden.
options: Arrange a GP-led family meeting that includes a social care needs assessment and a formal plan
Let the nearby adult child manage indefinitely without a plan
Tell the distant adult child what they are failing to do
Move the parent without their agreement to resolve the disagreement
payload.explanation: A GP-led family meeting with a formal needs assessment removes the disagreement from subjective opinion and grounds it in professional assessment.

payload.snippet: A joint venture between two companies has produced a significant intellectual property asset and both companies now claim full ownership without a clear contract clause covering this situation.
options: Engage a neutral IP lawyer to review the contributions and draft a co-ownership agreement
Publish the IP under one company's name before the other acts
Accept the ambiguity and proceed without any agreement
Dissolve the joint venture and abandon the IP entirely
payload.explanation: A co-ownership agreement is faster and cheaper than litigation and preserves both companies' ability to use the asset.

payload.snippet: Your family has one car, two car users, and a third adult in the household who needs a car for a new job starting next week.
options: Explore short-term car sharing or hire arrangements while the household agrees a long-term plan
Give the car to the person with the new job and everyone else adjusts
Tell the new employee to find a job closer to home
Buy a second car on finance before a long-term plan is agreed
payload.explanation: Short-term hire creates breathing space to make a considered long-term decision rather than an impulsive purchase.

payload.snippet: A co-authored research paper is ready for submission and the two authors are in a genuine disagreement about the significance of the findings that affects the framing of the abstract.
options: Each author writes their preferred abstract and the journal editor is asked to advise on which framing is more supported by the data
Publish the paper under one author's name only
Remove the contested finding from the paper entirely
Submit two separate papers with the same data
payload.explanation: Asking the journal editor to adjudicate is both faster and more authoritative than the authors resolving a scientific framing dispute between themselves.

payload.snippet: A volunteer has been managing a community project for three years and is burning out but refuses to step back because they fear the project will collapse without them.
options: Work with the volunteer to identify and train a deputy over two months so they can step back safely
Force the volunteer to resign before they are ready
Let the volunteer continue without addressing the burnout
Run the project yourself while the volunteer recovers
payload.explanation: Training a deputy respects the volunteer's contribution while creating the safety net they need to step back sustainably.

payload.snippet: Two school governors are deadlocked on whether to approve a controversial school expansion and their procedural rules require unanimous agreement at this stage.
options: Request that the full governing body meet to vote on whether to revise the unanimity requirement for this specific decision
Accept the deadlock and block the expansion by default
Persuade one governor to change their vote through informal pressure
Proceed with the expansion and address the governance breach later
payload.explanation: A full governing body vote on whether to revise the unanimity rule is the correct procedural response to a deadlock that is blocking a significant decision.

payload.snippet: A household pet that both members of a separating couple adopted together needs a new permanent home and both want to keep the pet but only one home is suitable.
options: Agree on the primary home for the pet and a visiting arrangement for the other person
U
payload.explanation: The pet's welfare is the primary consideration — the most suitable home should have primary care and the other person should retain access.

payload.snippet: An inheritance includes a collection of valuable artworks and two siblings want different items from the collection while a third wants the whole collection sold.
options: Engage an estates solicitor to conduct a formal valuation and allocation process that honours all three interests
Let the most emotionally invested sibling take everything
Sell everything and split the proceeds equally without asking what anyone wants
Allow each sibling to take one item secretly before the estate is valued
payload.explanation: A formal valuation and allocation process gives each sibling a clear process and prevents covert removal of assets before the estate is properly valued.

payload.snippet: You are a school principal and a significant proportion of students are consistently arriving late in the mornings, affecting attendance data and the quality of the first lesson, despite multiple reminders sent to parents.
options: Commission a survey of late-arriving families to identify the actual barriers before implementing any new policy
Issue detention for every late arrival starting next week
Move the first lesson to a low-stakes activity to absorb the lateness
Simply record the lateness without taking any action to identify the cause
payload.explanation: Surveying the actual barriers before applying sanctions prevents punishing families for structural problems they cannot solve with will alone.

payload.snippet: You are a GP and a patient has presented for their third appointment this year with symptoms of extreme morning fatigue that they describe as inability to function before 11am despite adequate sleep and no identified medical cause on two previous investigations.
options: Request thyroid function tests and a cortisol morning level blood draw before the next appointment
Advise the patient that they are naturally a late riser
Prescribe a stimulant to improve morning function
Tell the patient to book an earlier appointment time to force morning wakefulness
payload.explanation: Morning fatigue unresponsive to sleep improvement and not yet investigated hormonally warrants thyroid and cortisol testing — these are the two most common overlooked medical causes.

payload.snippet: A large organisation is planning a mandatory 7am all-staff call every Monday as a cultural alignment initiative and several employees with caring responsibilities and disability adjustments have said this is impossible for them.
options: Conduct an equality impact assessment and provide a recorded version with an alternative participation window
Cancel the initiative because some people cannot attend
Make attendance mandatory and manage individual exceptions informally
Move the call to 9am without further assessment of whether that also creates barriers
payload.explanation: An equality impact assessment identifies who is affected before the policy launches — a recorded alternative with a participation window is the legal reasonable adjustment.

payload.snippet: Your elderly parent with early-stage dementia requires a consistent and predictable morning routine to manage the condition but they are refusing help from the care agency staff and insisting on managing alone, causing daily safety concerns.
options: Consult the memory clinic about a supported decision-making approach and work with the care agency on a dementia-specific communication strategy
Remove all morning independence to guarantee safety
Accept the refusals and reduce the care agency visits
Ask a GP to assess whether the parent still has capacity to refuse care
payload.explanation: Supported decision-making with dementia-specific communication preserves autonomy while managing safety more effectively than either full removal of independence or unchecked refusals.

payload.snippet: A professional athlete's training schedule requires a two-hour morning session but they have been travelling across time zones for competitions and their circadian rhythm is consistently misaligned with the training time.
options: Work with the sports physiologist to implement a structured zeitgeber protocol — light therapy, meal timing, and temperature manipulation — before the next competition cycle
Skip morning training until the jet lag resolves
Move the training to the evening for the next three months
Accept the performance cost of misaligned training indefinitely
payload.explanation: Zeitgeber protocols are the evidence-based approach to circadian realignment for athletes — skipping or moving training does not address the underlying rhythm disruption.

payload.snippet: A household with a shift worker, a school-age child, and an early-starting remote worker has found that the three incompatible morning schedules are creating daily conflict over shared resources and noise.
options: Map each person's needs and constraints and create a household morning charter that protects each person's critical window
Ask the person whose shift starts earliest to move their schedule
Prioritise the child's school schedule as the anchor for all decisions
Accept the daily conflict as unavoidable in a mixed-schedule household
payload.explanation: A charter that maps everyone's constraints produces a solution that protects the most critical window for each person — something neither unilateral prioritisation nor passive acceptance achieves.

payload.snippet: Your company is being acquired and on the first morning of the integration process you discover that the incoming team has been given conflicting briefings about the new morning workflow that directly contradict what your team was told yesterday.
options: Email all parties a factual summary of both versions and request a joint clarification call before your team begins any workflow changes
Proceed with the version your team was briefed on and deal with the conflict later
Ask your team to wait for further instruction without contacting the incoming team
Follow the incoming team's version to signal cooperation
payload.explanation: A written summary of the conflict plus a joint clarification call surfaces the discrepancy before any work is done under a potentially incorrect process.

payload.snippet: A child with sensory processing disorder is consistently overwhelmed by the morning routine and the family has tried multiple strategies over two years without lasting improvement.
options: Request an occupational therapy assessment specifically focused on the sensory demands of the morning routine
Accept that mornings will always be chaotic for this child
Reduce the demands on the child by removing all non-essential morning steps permanently
Use reward charts for the fifth time despite their previous ineffectiveness
payload.explanation: An OT assessment of the specific sensory demands of the morning routine often identifies one or two environmental triggers that no amount of behavioural strategy can address.

payload.snippet: You are a hotel general manager and your breakfast service has received three consecutive negative guest reviews citing cold food, long waits, and disorganised service despite no change in staffing since the reviews were positive.
options: Conduct a covert observation of the full morning service from arrival to plate clearance and debrief the kitchen and floor teams separately
Threaten disciplinary action for the next negative review
Hire additional staff to absorb any shortfall
Reply to the reviews online and apologise without investigating the cause
payload.explanation: A covert observation across the full service arc is the only way to identify where in the complex morning workflow the failure is occurring before any operational change is made.

payload.snippet: A parent is consistently late to work every Monday morning because the childcare handover with an ex-partner runs over, and the ex-partner has started using the handover as an opportunity to discuss disputes about the custody arrangement.
options: Agree with the ex-partner that the handover is a child-focused transition only and redirect all co-parenting disputes to a scheduled weekly call
Arrive later every Monday and accept the professional consequences
Stop attending the handover yourself and send a family member instead
Take legal action to move the handover to a contact centre
payload.explanation: Agreeing a child-focused handover with a separate scheduled dispute time is the interpersonal boundary that directly solves the Monday lateness without requiring legal escalation.

payload.snippet: A start-up company's daily 8am standup has become a ninety-minute meeting and team energy and output on the days it runs are measurably lower than on days it is cancelled.
options: Implement a strict fifteen-minute facilitated format with a parking lot for items that need longer discussion
Cancel the standup permanently and move to asynchronous updates
Move the standup to midday to avoid morning energy drain
Let the standup run as long as it needs because cutting it feels disrespectful
payload.explanation: A strict format with a parking lot preserves the connection purpose of a daily standup while removing the energy cost of an unstructured long meeting.

payload.snippet: You are a long-distance lorry driver who has been asked by a dispatcher to start a route two hours earlier than scheduled without adequate rest between shifts, and the delivery is time-sensitive for the client.
options: Decline the earlier start, cite your mandatory rest period, and offer the earliest safe departure time
Start early because the client delivery matters
Drive the first two hours then take a rest break en route
Call in sick rather than refuse the shift directly
payload.explanation: Commercial drivers have legally mandated rest periods — driving without them is both illegal and the most common cause of fatal lorry accidents.

payload.snippet: A child at a boarding school has been consistently reporting morning headaches and nausea on school days only and the school medical team has attributed it to anxiety, but the symptoms have persisted for two terms.
options: Request a GP appointment to rule out a physical cause and ask the school medical team to share their records
Accept the school's anxiety diagnosis without a GP review
Remove the child from boarding school based on the symptoms alone
Increase the child's anxiety management programme at school
payload.explanation: Two terms of physical symptoms attributed to anxiety without a GP review is insufficient investigation — carbon monoxide, a dietary trigger, or a structural condition at the school building should be ruled out.

payload.snippet: A hospital department has found that morning handovers between night and day shifts are generating a high rate of communication errors and two near-miss incidents in the past month have been traced to handover failures.
options: Implement a structured SBAR handover tool with a mandatory read-back check and run a simulation exercise before deployment
Move all handovers to an electronic system immediately
Extend the handover period from fifteen to thirty minutes
Investigate the two near-misses in isolation without changing the handover structure
payload.explanation: An SBAR structured handover with read-back confirmation is the NHS evidence-based gold standard for reducing verbal handover errors in clinical settings.

payload.snippet: You are a project manager and your most productive team member consistently underperforms in morning meetings but produces their best work in the afternoon and has asked to shift their start time to 10am which conflicts with team norms.
options: Trial a 10am start for a fixed period with agreed output metrics and review the impact on team productivity
Deny the request to preserve team norm consistency
Approve the shift permanently without defining success metrics
Ask the team member to attend morning meetings remotely from home and start effectively at 10am
payload.explanation: A fixed-period trial with defined output metrics creates evidence for a permanent decision rather than a policy based purely on norm conformity.

payload.snippet: A family home has been found to have a high level of carbon dioxide build-up in the bedrooms overnight due to inadequate ventilation, and family members have been experiencing morning headaches and fatigue for months.
options: Improve bedroom ventilation immediately and book a professional indoor air quality assessment
Paint the walls with special paint to absorb CO2
Accept morning tiredness as a family trait
Buy a carbon dioxide monitor but take no immediate action
payload.explanation: Immediate ventilation improvement reduces the acute risk while a professional assessment identifies the source and long-term fix.

payload.snippet: A large open-plan office has been redesigned to reduce cubicle space and the increased noise in the morning when the first team arrives has measurably reduced individual output on tasks requiring concentration.
options: Create a morning quiet zone policy for the first ninety minutes of the working day
Move all concentration tasks to the afternoon permanently
Provide noise-cancelling headphones and leave the noise unaddressed
Allow each team to self-manage their noise level
payload.explanation: A morning quiet zone policy is the collective solution — individual headphones without a policy normalise the noise source rather than addressing it.

payload.snippet: A teenager has been reporting significant morning anxiety every school day for a full term and a half and the school counsellor has suggested strategies that have not worked over eight weeks.
options: Request a referral to CAMHS via the GP and document the school counsellor's strategies and their failure to inform the referral
Keep trying the school counsellor's strategies for another term
Remove the teenager from school to eliminate the morning trigger
Dismiss the anxiety as exam stress that will self-resolve
payload.explanation: Eight weeks of ineffective counselling with persistent daily anxiety meets the threshold for a CAMHS referral — continuing the same ineffective intervention without escalation is not clinically appropriate.

payload.snippet: Your organisation has introduced a 7:30am fire drill rotation that requires all staff to be present but several remote workers who live forty minutes away cannot always arrive by 7:30 without significant personal cost.
options: Propose a split drill with an in-person session at 9am and a remote walkthrough at 7:30 for those affected
Require all staff to attend the 7:30 drill regardless of distance
Exempt remote workers from all fire drill requirements
Move the drill to lunchtime for everyone to accommodate the remote workers
payload.explanation: A split format honours the health and safety requirement for all staff while acknowledging the genuine barrier that distance creates for some.

payload.snippet: A care home resident with advanced Parkinson's disease has a morning medication window of ninety minutes when the medication is most effective and the care home's staffing rota consistently means the medication is given outside this window.
options: Escalate to the clinical lead with a documented record of timing failures and request a care plan amendment that prioritises the medication window in the rota
Accept the timing variations as unavoidable in a busy home
Ask the resident's family to administer the medication themselves
Reduce the medication dose to reduce the impact of timing variations
payload.explanation: Documented evidence of a consistent medication timing failure gives the clinical lead the specific information needed to create a rota-level fix rather than a case-by-case workaround.

payload.snippet: Leo's close friend dares him to steal a small item from the cafeteria line as a joke, insisting that everyone does it and no one ever gets caught.
options: refuses the dare and explains clearly that stealing is wrong
steals a small item to prove he is brave enough
steals something but feels guilty and secretly puts it back
tells a teacher about the dare without first refusing himself
payload.explanation: Refusing a dare that involves stealing shows strong moral character.

payload.snippet: Mia finds out that the classmate who mocked her packed lunch last week has now forgotten their own lunch and is sitting there hungry.
options: offers to share some of her food generously anyway
tells the classmate this is what they deserve for being unkind
ignores the classmate since they were unkind to her before
shares food only if the classmate apologises to her first
payload.explanation: Being kind even to someone who was unkind before shows genuine generosity.

payload.snippet: Kai notices his friend has been skipping lunch for three days in a row and is looking tired, pale, and dizzy each afternoon.
options: privately tells a trusted teacher about his concern
confronts his friend loudly about it in front of everyone
says nothing since it is none of his business to interfere
tells all his friends as an interesting piece of gossip
payload.explanation: Discreetly telling a trusted adult is the responsible thing when a friend may be struggling.

payload.snippet: Nina is on a strict medical diet and a well-meaning teacher insists she try the dessert being offered at today's special lunch.
options: politely but firmly explains her medical dietary restrictions
eats the dessert to avoid disappointing the teacher today
lies and says she already had some from somewhere else
gets upset and refuses to speak about her diet at all
payload.explanation: Calmly explaining a medical need is both honest and necessary for wellbeing.

payload.snippet: Tom watches an older student push in at the front of the queue and take the last portion of the only food Tom can eat due to his allergies.
options: asks a staff member calmly for help resolving the situation
pushes the older student out of the queue in anger
shouts at the older student loudly in front of everyone
takes someone else's food since he now has none because of this
payload.explanation: Asking a staff member to help resolve a queue conflict is the correct action.

payload.snippet: Ava's friend group begins saying loudly that anyone who eats healthy food is just trying too hard to impress their parents.
options: disagrees and explains calmly that eating well is important for health
agrees with her friends just to fit in and stay popular
stops eating her healthy food and hides it away in shame
starts eating differently to match whatever her friends think is cool
payload.explanation: Standing up for healthy eating against peer pressure shows confidence and good judgment.

payload.snippet: Ben discovers that his lunch was stolen from the shared classroom fridge and he now has absolutely nothing to eat.
options: tells a teacher and reports what happened calmly
searches through other children's bags to find his missing food
takes a random person's food as a fair replacement
gets angry and immediately accuses his closest friend without evidence
payload.explanation: Reporting the theft calmly to a teacher is the correct and fair approach.

payload.snippet: Grace watches a child at the next table eat something and immediately start coughing very badly and turning red.
options: tells a teacher immediately that the child needs help urgently
waits to see if the child gets better on their own first
tells her friends loudly to look at the child who is unwell
panics very loudly and upsets the other children nearby
payload.explanation: Alerting a teacher immediately is the right and urgent action when someone seems unwell.

payload.snippet: Max finds out after eating that the cafeteria sold him something containing an allergen that was not listed on the label anywhere.
options: tells a teacher and the cafeteria staff about it immediately
hopes the unlisted allergen is just a tiny trace amount
throws the packaging away without mentioning it to anyone
posts about the mistake online to warn other students himself
payload.explanation: Reporting the allergen labelling error protects Max and every other student with allergies.

payload.snippet: Lily has one last piece of her favourite food and both her best friend and a younger child who forgot their lunch both ask for it.
options: gives it to the younger child who has no food at all today
gives it to her best friend since they are much closer to her
eats it herself since she is not actually required to share
breaks it in two and gives a small piece to each of them
payload.explanation: Giving food to the child who has nothing is the most generous and fair decision.

payload.snippet: Zoe realises she accidentally ate her friend's lunch, and her friend has a serious nut allergy — and her own food also contains nuts.
options: tells her friend and a teacher immediately to prevent any harm
says nothing since she is not completely sure about the allergy details
tells only her friend very quietly and hopes it is not serious
waits until after lunch to check whether her friend seems okay
payload.explanation: This is a potential medical emergency — telling a teacher immediately is absolutely vital.

payload.snippet: Sam's lunch contains a cultural dish from his background and a group of children begin to loudly mock it in front of the whole table.
options: calmly explains what the dish is and its cultural significance
throws the food away to make the mockery stop right away
insults the other children's lunches right back in retaliation
cries and asks to be excused from the cafeteria entirely
payload.explanation: Calmly educating others about your culture is a powerful and dignified response.

payload.snippet: Finn is being pressured by his friends to hand over his lunch to an older student who is demanding food from younger children.
options: refuses to give his food and tells a trusted adult about the situation
gives his lunch away to avoid any confrontation with the older student
asks his friends to hand over their lunches instead of his
challenges the older student directly to a debate about fairness
payload.explanation: Refusing and reporting to an adult is the right response to an intimidating situation.

payload.snippet: Ruby notices a lunch staff member appear to sneeze directly onto the food being served and then immediately carry on serving other students.
options: politely tells a different staff member what she witnessed
refuses all food and goes hungry without saying anything to anyone
shouts out loudly about what happened right in front of everyone
eats the food anyway and hopes the contamination does not matter
payload.explanation: Politely informing another staff member is the responsible hygiene action.

payload.snippet: Owen finds a note in his lunchbox from a classmate claiming they swapped his food and asking him to look inside their bag.
options: shows the note to a teacher before opening any unfamiliar bag
opens the bag himself to investigate without telling anyone first
confronts the classmate loudly about the note in the cafeteria
ignores the note entirely and throws both the note and his lunchbox away
payload.explanation: Telling a teacher before investigating is the safe and responsible approach to an unusual situation.

payload.snippet: Sophie discovers that today's school hot lunch contained an ingredient she is intolerant to and she has already started eating it.
options: stops eating immediately and tells a teacher right away
finishes the meal since she has already started eating it now
drinks lots of water hoping it will somehow reduce the reaction
tells her friends loudly that the school food is dangerous for her
payload.explanation: Stopping and telling a teacher is the safest response to a discovered dietary problem mid-meal.

payload.snippet: Jake's friend says he is not hungry at lunch but Jake can see the friend shaking slightly and looking very pale.
options: gently encourages his friend to eat at least something small
leaves his friend alone entirely since he said he is not hungry
tells everyone nearby loudly that their friend looks very ill
pushes all of his own food immediately in front of his friend
payload.explanation: Gently encouraging a friend who may have low blood sugar shows care and good judgment.

payload.snippet: Chloe sees another student saving a seat but the person the seat was saved for never arrives and other students are left standing with no seat.
options: tells the student saving the seat that others need somewhere to sit
takes the saved seat herself even though she knows it was reserved
tells a teacher that someone is being unfair about the seating
stands at the edge of the room eating and does not eat properly
payload.explanation: Communicating with the seat-saver is the fair and direct way to solve the problem.

payload.snippet: Ethan realises he made his friend feel really bad earlier by joking about their packed lunch loudly in front of others.
options: goes to his friend at lunch and sincerely apologises to them directly
ignores what he said and hopes his friend has already forgotten it
makes another joke about it to try to lighten the mood between them
asks a mutual friend to pass on his apology so he does not have to
payload.explanation: A sincere direct apology is the most respectful and effective way to repair a friendship.

payload.snippet: Isla is being pressured by her diet-obsessed friend to throw her whole lunch away and pretend she is not hungry.
options: refuses and explains clearly that eating properly is important for her health
throws her lunch away to keep her friend happy for just one day
agrees but secretly eats her lunch hiding in a bathroom stall alone
tells her friend bluntly that they have a very unhealthy attitude about food
payload.explanation: Refusing to skip meals due to peer pressure shows respect for your own health and wellbeing.

payload.snippet: Leo is on the bus when an older student tells him to hold a suspicious-looking package for them until the next stop, saying it is just a phone but it does not look like one.
options: refuses clearly and immediately tells the driver what happened
holds it briefly to avoid a confrontation with the older student
opens the package to see what is actually inside it
puts the package on the seat and moves away without telling anyone
payload.explanation: Refusing and telling the driver is the correct response — never hold unknown items from strangers.

payload.snippet: Mia is on the school bus when she witnesses the driver using a mobile phone while driving and the bus swerves slightly to one side.
options: calmly tells the driver to stop using the phone and then reports it to a teacher
says nothing since she does not want to get the driver in trouble
shouts at the driver loudly in a way that might distract them further
takes a photo of the driver using the phone as evidence
payload.explanation: Calmly addressing the driver and then reporting it protects everyone's safety now and in the future.

payload.snippet: Kai is on the bus when his friend group starts excluding a newer classmate and encouraging others not to let him sit with them.
options: refuses to join in the exclusion and invites the student to sit with him
goes along with the exclusion to stay on good terms with his friends
tells the excluded student privately that he is sorry but cannot help right now
tells a teacher when he arrives at school but does not help during the journey
payload.explanation: Refusing to participate and actively including the student is the bravest and most impactful choice.

payload.snippet: Nina is on the bus when a man she does not know sits very close to her despite empty seats and begins asking her uncomfortable personal questions.
options: moves to sit near the driver and quietly tells them she feels uncomfortable
answers his questions politely since it is rude to ignore an adult
loudly tells him to go away and sit somewhere else
texts her parent to come and meet the bus but says nothing to the driver
payload.explanation: Moving to sit near the driver and alerting them discreetly is the safest response.

payload.snippet: Tom gets off the bus with friends and then realises one of his friends stole a phone from another passenger during the journey.
options: tells his friend to return the phone or he will report it
says nothing since his friend already got off and the passenger has not noticed
agrees to help his friend hide the phone so they are not caught
reports it to the bus company immediately without giving his friend a chance to return it
payload.explanation: Telling his friend to return it gives them a chance to do the right thing — escalating if they refuse is correct.

payload.snippet: Ava witnesses a serious physical fight between two adults on the bus that is frightening younger passengers nearby.
options: stays calm, stays seated, and calls emergency services if the situation is dangerous
tries to physically step in between the fighting adults
gets off the bus immediately at the next stop even though it is not hers
shouts at the adults fighting to try to help the young children nearby
payload.explanation: Staying safe and contacting emergency services is the correct response to a serious altercation.

payload.snippet: Ben is on the bus when his friend begins to feel very ill and says they think they might faint.
options: tells the driver immediately and helps his friend stay as calm and still as possible
tries to carry his friend off the bus at the next stop on his own
calls his own parent first for advice before alerting the driver
gives his friend water and sweets and just hopes that will be enough
payload.explanation: Alerting the driver immediately ensures the right help is provided quickly.

payload.snippet: Grace overhears a passenger on the phone making plans she believes involve hurting a student who goes to her school.
options: tells a trusted teacher about what she heard as soon as she arrives at school
tries to record the phone conversation as evidence before acting
approaches the person to confirm what she heard before deciding what to do
texts the person she thinks might be in danger straight away
payload.explanation: Telling a trusted teacher means a responsible adult can assess and act on the concern appropriately.

payload.snippet: Max is on the bus when the driver appears lost and is clearly driving in completely the wrong direction.
options: politely approaches the driver and mentions that the route seems different today
says nothing and assumes the driver knows something the passengers do not
gets all the passengers to shout directions to the driver from their seats
calls his parents to come and collect him from wherever the bus ends up
payload.explanation: Calmly informing the driver is the most helpful action — they may have simply missed a turn.

payload.snippet: Lily sees a classmate on the bus posting something deeply unkind about another student in their class on a group chat.
options: asks her classmate to delete the post and speaks to a teacher about it
takes a screenshot and shares it further to show what the classmate did
says nothing since online activity has nothing to do with what happens on the bus
replies to the group chat herself publicly defending the student being targeted
payload.explanation: Asking for deletion and involving a teacher is the most effective way to address cyberbullying.

payload.snippet: Zoe is on the bus when she spots that the door is not fully closed and has been rattling open slightly as the bus moves along.
options: tells the driver immediately so the door can be secured safely
moves away from the door but says nothing to the driver about it
uses her bag to wedge the door closed herself
asks another passenger to hold the door closed for the rest of the journey
payload.explanation: Telling the driver immediately ensures the safety hazard is fixed properly.

payload.snippet: Sam is on the bus and notices that the passenger in the disabled priority seat will not move for an elderly woman who clearly needs to sit down.
options: politely asks the person if they would consider giving up the seat for the elderly woman
tells the elderly woman loudly that the person is being very selfish
reports it straight to the driver without addressing it with the passenger first
gives up his own seat rather than getting involved in the situation
payload.explanation: Politely asking is the direct and respectful first step before escalating to the driver.

payload.snippet: Finn is on the bus when he finds a bag someone left and, looking inside for identification, he discovers what looks like an unattended suspicious item.
options: does not touch the bag, moves away, and tells the driver immediately
removes the suspicious item and throws it out of the window
opens the bag further to investigate whether it is actually dangerous
quietly gets off at the next stop and calls emergency services without telling the driver
payload.explanation: Not touching the bag and immediately alerting the driver is the correct response.

payload.snippet: Ruby is on the bus when she notices a passenger trying to access another person's laptop bag while that person has headphones on and is completely unaware.
options: tells the driver or alerts the laptop owner quietly and directly
watches without acting since she might have misunderstood what she saw
shouts out loudly accusing the person before confirming what she witnessed
takes a photo as evidence before deciding how to act on the situation
payload.explanation: Acting quickly to alert either the driver or the victim protects the person's property.

payload.snippet: Owen's bus is caught in severe traffic and he will clearly miss his connecting bus home with no other option available.
options: calls his parents calmly to explain the delay and arrange alternative transport
gets off the bus in heavy traffic and tries to walk along the road
demands the bus driver use a faster route immediately to get through
starts crying and repeatedly checks his phone without doing anything practical
payload.explanation: Calling parents calmly to arrange alternative help is the safest and most practical response.

payload.snippet: Sophie's friend encourages her to skip paying the bus fare by slipping past the driver while another passenger distracts them.
options: refuses and pays her fare as normal
goes along with the plan since it is just a small amount of money
refuses but stays silent about the fact that her friend skipped the fare
refuses and immediately tells the driver that her friend skipped the fare
payload.explanation: Refusing to skip the fare is the right thing to do — it is dishonest regardless of the amount.

payload.snippet: Jake gets on the bus and hears a child near the back making threats to another passenger who looks frightened.
options: tells the driver immediately and quietly from his position
walks to the back of the bus and tells the threatening child to stop
sits down and watches to see if the situation worsens before acting
asks his friends to go with him to confront the child as a group
payload.explanation: Telling the driver immediately means someone in authority handles it safely.

payload.snippet: Chloe is on the bus when heavy rain starts and the driver briefly loses control on a slippery road before regaining it.
options: stays calm, stays seated with her belt fastened, and follows any instructions
demands the driver pull over and let everyone off immediately
